title: Kids' Vaping Linked to Smoking, Health Issues
paragraphs: Vaping is often promoted as a less harmful alternative to smoking for adults who want to quit. However, a major new review from the UK has found clear links between vaping and a range of health problems among children and young people, as well as an increased likelihood that they will go on to smoke cigarettes.

The review, led by Paula Oyella, was published in the journal Archives of Disease in Childhood in August 2026. The journal is co-owned by the BMJ group and the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health (RCPCH), which represents children's doctors in the UK. The researchers identified more than 14,000 published articles, examined 325 studies in detail and finally combined the evidence from 81 studies. These studies looked at the effects of vaping on people aged up to 19, covering eight different areas of health and social life.

The review found consistent evidence that vaping is linked to poorer respiratory health. Young people who vape reported more coughing, wheezing and symptoms of bronchitis, and those with asthma experienced more frequent attacks. In addition, long-term studies provided strong evidence that young people who vape are significantly more likely to start smoking cigarettes later.

Vaping was also linked to anxiety, depression and suicidal thoughts, as well as to problems with oral and dental health. Furthermore, the researchers found emerging evidence that vaping may affect sleep, eye health and allergies, but more research is needed in these areas.
According to the RCPCH, experimentation with vaping and regular use among young people have increased around tenfold over the past decade, and vaping often begins in early adolescence.

Professor Will Carroll, one of the review's authors, said that vaping should not be seen as a harmless part of growing up. Carroll called on the government to go further, for example by limiting the types of vape flavors that can be sold, rather than only restricting how they are described. Dr. Mike McKean of the RCPCH pointed out that because vaping is relatively new, there is still much that is not known about its long-term effects on children.
It is important to note that most of the studies in the review were observational, which means that they show links rather than proving that vaping causes these problems.
